title: The Mid-Luteal Challenge: Tough Even for Automated Insulin Delivery Systems
content: Background: Menstrual cycle–related glycaemic fluctuations may persist despite automated insulin delivery (AID), yet evidence in adolescents remains limited. Our aim was to evaluate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics across five menstrual cycle phases and examine insulin delivery and meal-related parameters among AID users. Methods: Adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D), regular menstrual cycles, available CGM data, and menstrual cycle records were included. Glycaemic outcomes included Time in Range (TIR), Time Above Range (TAR), Time Below Range (TBR), and coefficient of variation across five predefined menstrual phases. In AID users, insulin delivery, meal announcements, and carbohydrate intake were also evaluated. Results: Twenty-nine adolescents with T1D (mean age:15.6±2.2 years) contributing 107 menstrual cycles were included. The mid-luteal phase showed the least favourable glycaemic profile, with lower TIR (67.4%) than the early follicular (69.5%), mid-follicular (73.1%), peri-ovulatory (71.3%), and late luteal (70.1%) phases. Compared with non-AID therapy, AID systems were associated with higher TIR throughout the menstrual cycle and significantly lower exposure to mild hypoglycaemia. Among AID users, the mid- and late luteal phases showed increased insulin delivery, higher bolus proportion, and greater carbohydrate intake. Conclusions: Glycaemic control varies across the menstrual cycle in adolescent girls with T1D. Although AID systems improve overall regulation, cycle-related variability persists, supporting individualized phase-specific insulin management strategies.
